questions.question: Complete the table of successive ionisation energies of nitrogen (the table values are shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: log (ionisation energy): 6th = 4.73 and 7th = 4.81
steps: Take log10 of each missing ionisation energy.
log10(53 268) = 4.73 and log10(64 362) = 4.81, both to 2 decimal places like the other entries.

questions.question: Plot a graph of log(ionisation energy) against ionisation number for nitrogen (the data are shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: Graph of log (ionisation energy) against ionisation number: seven points from 3.15 at 1 to 4.81 at 7, with a large jump between the 5th and 6th points
steps: Put ionisation number (1 to 7) on the x-axis and log (ionisation energy / kJ mol^-1) on the y-axis, with labelled axes and a y-scale from 3.0 to 5.0 so the points fill the grid.
Join the points with straight lines (or a smooth line); the first five rise gradually, then there is a big step up between 5 and 6 and a small rise from 6 to 7.

questions.question: Give a reason why the logarithm of the ionisation energy, rather than the ionisation energy itself, is used to plot this graph.
questions.answer: Ionisation energies cover a very wide range of values, so the logarithm compresses the scale and allows all the values to be shown on one graph.
steps: Successive ionisation energies range from about 1400 to over 1 000 000 kJ mol-1.
A log scale turns this huge range into a manageable range of values.
So small and large values can both be plotted clearly.

questions.question: Explain what can be deduced from the graph about the electronic structure of nitrogen. (The graph is shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: Nitrogen has 5 electrons in its outer shell (the second shell) and 2 in the inner shell, so its electronic structure is 2,5
steps: The first five points rise gradually, so these five electrons are removed from the same (outer) shell.
There is a very large jump between the 5th and 6th ionisation energies, so the 6th electron comes from a shell closer to the nucleus, which is not shielded: nitrogen has 5 outer electrons (Group 5).
The 6th and 7th values are close together (4.73 and 4.81), so there are 2 electrons in the innermost shell: structure 2,5, i.e. 1s2 2s2 2p3.

questions.question: Explain why the first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen.
questions.answer: Oxygen has a pair of electrons in one 2p orbital, and repulsion between the paired electrons makes one easier to remove; nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p3 with no pairs.
steps: Nitrogen is 2p3, with one electron in each 2p orbital, which is a stable arrangement.
Oxygen is 2p4, so one 2p orbital holds two electrons.
Repulsion between these paired electrons makes one easier to remove, so O has a lower first IE than N.

questions.topic: Dot And Cross Diagram Of N2
questions.question: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram to show the bonding in a molecule of nitrogen, N2.
questions.answer: N=N shown as a triple covalent bond (N#N): three shared pairs of electrons between the two N atoms, each N with one lone pair (N:::N with one lone pair on each atom).
steps: Each N atom has 5 outer electrons, needing 3 more to complete an octet.
Each N shares 3 electrons with the other N, forming three shared pairs (a triple bond).
Each N atom keeps one lone pair of 2 electrons, giving 8 electrons around each atom.

questions.topic: Number Of Atoms In Nitrogen Gas
questions.question: Calculate the number of nitrogen atoms in 5.60 g of nitrogen gas. Avogadro constant = 6.02 x 10^23 mol-1.
questions.answer: 2.41 x 10^23 atoms
steps: Each N2 molecule contains 2 atoms, so moles of N atoms = 0.400 mol.

questions.topic: Moles Of Nitrogen From Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: A sample of nitrogen gas occupied 108 cm3 at 25 C and 1.36 x 10^5 Pa. Using pV = nRT with R = 8.31 J K-1 mol-1, calculate the number of moles of nitrogen.
steps: Rearrange: n = pV / RT.

questions.question: State the number and type of each of the particles in the nucleus of a chlorine-35 atom.
questions.answer: 17 protons and 18 neutrons
steps: Chlorine has atomic number 17, so 17 protons.
Neutrons = mass number - protons = 35 - 17 = 18.

questions.question: Complete the electronic configuration of a chloride ion, Cl-, using the s, p, d notation, given that it starts 1s2.
steps: Chlorine has 17 electrons, so Cl- has 18.
After 1s2 the next are 2s2 (4), 2p6 (10), 3s2 (12), 3p6 (18).
Full configuration: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6.

questions.question: A sample of chlorine contains 75.53% of chlorine-35 atoms (the rest is chlorine-37). Calculate the relative atomic mass to two decimal places.

questions.topic: Dot And Cross Diagram Of ClF3
questions.question: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for chlorine trifluoride, ClF3, showing outer shell electrons only.
questions.answer: Central Cl with three single covalent bonds to F atoms and two lone pairs on Cl; each F has three lone pairs and one bonding pair.
steps: Cl has 7 outer electrons and each F has 7.
Cl forms 3 covalent bonds (one shared pair each to F), using 3 of its electrons, leaving 4 electrons, i.e. 2 lone pairs.
Each F shares one pair with Cl and has three lone pairs, completing its octet.

questions.question: State, in terms of electrons, what is unusual about the dot-and-cross diagram you have drawn for ClF3.
questions.answer: The central chlorine atom has more than 8 electrons (10) in its outer shell, an expanded octet.
steps: Cl has 7 outer electrons; 3 are used for bonds and 4 are lone pairs.
Counting shared pairs and lone pairs around Cl gives 10 electrons in its outer shell.
This is an expanded octet, which is possible for elements in Period 3 and beyond.

questions.question: Complete the mass spectrum to show the peaks expected for the molecular ion ClF3+. Fluorine has one isotope, 19F. (The spectrum grid is shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: Two peaks: m/z 92 (35Cl19F3+) and m/z 94 (37Cl19F3+), in an approximate ratio of 3 : 1.
steps: Chlorine is about 75.5% 35Cl and 24.5% 37Cl, so the peak heights are about 3 : 1.
Each peak is singly charged, so the m/z values are 92 and 94.

questions.topic: Volume Of ClF3 From Ideal Gas Equation
questions.question: Calculate, using the ideal gas equation, the volume in cm3 occupied by 0.0200 mol of ClF3 gas at 60 C and 1.28 x 10^5 Pa. R = 8.31 J K-1 mol-1.

The bonding within an ammonium ion, NH4+, is formed by: A covalent bonding only; B covalent and dative covalent bonding only; C covalent and ionic bonding only; D covalent, dative covalent and ionic bonding.
questions.answer: B (covalent and dative covalent bonding only)
steps: NH4+ has three N-H covalent bonds formed from shared pairs.
The fourth N-H bond is dative covalent, with both shared electrons from N.
There is no ionic bonding within the ion itself; ionic bonding only occurs between separate ions in a salt.

questions.question: Which of these molecules is the most polar? A H-H; B H-F; C H-Cl; D H-Br.
questions.answer: B (H-F)
steps: Polarity depends on the electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms.
H-H is non-polar; F has the largest electronegativity, so the difference with H is greatest in H-F.
So H-F is the most polar.

questions.question: What is the polarity of the Al-Cl bond and the polarity of a trigonal planar AlCl3 molecule?
questions.answer: The Al-Cl bond is polar, but the trigonal planar AlCl3 molecule is non-polar because the bond dipoles cancel by symmetry.
steps: Cl is more electronegative than Al, so each Al-Cl bond is polar.
AlCl3 is trigonal planar, with three identical bonds at 120 degrees.
The three bond dipoles cancel, so the molecule is non-polar.

questions.question: Which is correct for tetrafluoromethane (CF4)? (The options are shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: C-F bonds are polar, but the tetrahedral CF4 molecule is non-polar because its bond dipoles cancel.
steps: F is more electronegative than C, so each C-F bond is polar.
CF4 is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so the four bond dipoles cancel out.
The molecule has no overall dipole and is non-polar.

questions.question: Which diagram best represents the electron density in a molecule of hydrogen chloride? (The diagram options are shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: D: overlapping clouds with the larger Cl cloud overlapping the smaller H cloud
steps: The H and Cl atoms share a pair of electrons, so their electron clouds overlap, which rules out A (separate clouds).
The chlorine atom is much larger and has more electron density than hydrogen, and it is more electronegative, so the cloud around Cl is bigger; this is shown in D.
C shows two clouds of nearly equal size (symmetrical sharing) and B is a single cloud with no clear difference between the atoms.

questions.question: Which of these does not have a structure formed by a giant lattice of carbon atoms? A C60 fullerene; B diamond; C graphene; D graphite.
questions.answer: A (C60 fullerene)
steps: Diamond, graphene and graphite all have giant covalent lattices of carbon atoms.
C60 fullerene is a discrete spherical molecule of 60 carbon atoms.
So C60 is the exception.

questions.topic: Polarity Of S-F Bond And SF6
questions.question: Which row gives the correct polarities of the S-F bond and the SF6 molecule? (The table of rows is shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: B: S-F bond polar, SF6 molecule non-polar
steps: Fluorine is more electronegative than sulfur, so each S-F bond is polar.
SF6 is a symmetrical octahedral molecule with six identical S-F bonds, so the dipoles cancel and the molecule is non-polar.

questions.question: Which compound has bonds that are the most polar? A H2O; B H2S; C NH3; D PH3.
questions.answer: A (H2O)
steps: Bond polarity depends on the electronegativity difference.
O has the highest electronegativity of the central atoms here, so O-H has the largest difference with H.
So H2O has the most polar bonds.

questions.question: Which of these molecules is the most polar? A HF; B OF2; C BF3; D CF4.
questions.answer: A (HF)
steps: BF3 and CF4 are symmetrical, so their bond dipoles cancel and they are non-polar.
OF2 is a bent molecule and is polar, but it has a smaller overall dipole than HF.
HF has a single strongly polar bond with a large electronegativity difference, so it has the largest dipole.

questions.topic: Relative Atomic Mass Of Silicon From Spectrum
questions.question: Calculate the relative atomic mass of silicon to two decimal places using the mass spectrum data (the data are shown in a figure shown in the figure below).
steps: The relative abundances add up to 92.17 + 4.71 + 3.12 = 100.00.

questions.question: Suggest a reason why there is a small peak in the mass spectrum of silicon at m/z = 14.
questions.answer: It is caused by a doubly charged ion, 28Si2+, which has m/z = 28 / 2 = 14.
steps: m/z = 14 with 2+ charge gives a mass of 28.
28Si is the most abundant silicon isotope, so 28Si2+ forms with a small abundance.
Doubly charged ions give peaks at half their mass, so this is a small peak from 28Si2+.

questions.topic: Protons And Neutrons Of Silicon Isotopes
questions.question: Complete the table to show the number of protons and neutrons in each isotope of silicon (the table and isotope mass numbers are shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: 28Si: 14 protons, 14 neutrons; 29Si: 14 protons, 15 neutrons; 30Si: 14 protons, 16 neutrons
steps: Silicon has atomic number 14, so every isotope has 14 protons.
Neutrons = mass number - 14: 28 - 14 = 14, 29 - 14 = 15 and 30 - 14 = 16.

questions.question: Silicon dioxide has a giant lattice like diamond and is used as a heat-resistant, electrically insulating layer on semiconductor devices. Explain how its structure and bonding make it useful for this application.
questions.answer: SiO2 is a giant covalent lattice with many strong covalent Si-O bonds, so it has a high melting temperature (heat resistant), and it has no mobile electrons or ions, so it is an electrical insulator.
steps: A giant covalent lattice needs a lot of energy to break many strong covalent Si-O bonds, so it is heat resistant.
All electrons are held in localised covalent bonds, so there are no free electrons or mobile ions.
With no mobile charge carriers, it cannot conduct electricity, so it insulates.

questions.question: A sample of calcium silicate contains 12.0 g of calcium, 8.43 g of silicon and 14.47 g of oxygen. Determine the empirical formula, showing working. Ar: Ca 40.1, Si 28.1, O 16.0.
questions.answer: CaSiO3
steps: Empirical formula = CaSiO3.

questions.topic: Volume Of CO2 At Low Temperature
questions.question: Calculate the volume in cm3 occupied by 3.00 g of CO2 at 5.0 C and 1.3 x 10^5 Pa, using pV = nRT with R = 8.31 J K-1 mol-1. Mr CO2 = 44.0.

questions.topic: Relative Formula Mass Of Double Salt
questions.question: What is the relative formula mass of the double salt (NH4)2Fe(SO4)2.6H2O? Options A 277.9, B 284.0, C 392.0, D 447.8.
What types of bond are present in ammonium sulfate? A ionic only; B covalent and ionic only; C dative covalent and ionic only; D ionic, covalent and dative covalent.
questions.answer: D (ionic, covalent and dative covalent)
steps: Ammonium sulfate contains NH4+ and SO4 2- ions, so there is ionic bonding between them.
Within NH4+, there are covalent and dative covalent N-H bonds.
Within SO4 2-, there are covalent bonds and dative covalent S=O bonds, so all three types are present.

questions.topic: Number Of Ions In Double Salt
questions.question: What is the total number of ions present in 0.1 mol of the double salt (NH4)2Fe(SO4)2.6H2O? L = 6.02 x 10^23 mol-1. Options A 1.80 x 10^23, B 2.41 x 10^23, C 3.01 x 10^23, D 6.62 x 10^23.
steps: Each formula unit contains 2 NH4+, 1 Fe2+ and 2 SO4 2-, giving 5 ions (the water is not ionised).
Ions per 0.1 mol = 0.1 x 5 = 0.5 mol of ions.

questions.question: Which substance has a giant lattice of atoms? A diamond; B ice; C poly(ethene); D sodium chloride.
questions.answer: A (diamond)
steps: Diamond is a giant covalent lattice of carbon atoms, with each C bonded to four others.
Ice and poly(ethene) are simple molecular structures (ice has molecules; poly(ethene) has long chains of molecules).
Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice, not of atoms, so the answer is diamond.

questions.question: Which of these molecules is not polar? A CO2; B HCl; C H2O; D NH3.
questions.answer: A (CO2)
steps: CO2 is linear and symmetrical, with two polar C=O bonds that cancel.
HCl, H2O and NH3 are asymmetric, so their bond dipoles do not cancel.
So CO2 is the non-polar molecule.

questions.question: At 180 C, aluminium chloride exists as Al2Cl6. What is the structure of Al2Cl6? (The options are shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: Two AlCl3 units joined by dative covalent bonds, forming a dimer with two bridging Cl atoms, so each Al is surrounded tetrahedrally by four Cl atoms (option C: the dative-bond arrows point from the bridging Cl atoms towards the Al atoms).
steps: Al in AlCl3 has only 6 electrons in its outer shell and is electron deficient.
A Cl atom on one AlCl3 donates a lone pair to the Al of another, forming dative covalent bonds.
This gives a dimer Al2Cl6 with two bridging Cl atoms and a tetrahedral environment around each Al.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term isotopes.
questions.answer: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons (different mass numbers).
steps: Isotopes are atoms of the same element.
They have the same number of protons, so the same atomic number.
They have different numbers of neutrons, so different mass numbers.

questions.question: Complete the table of subatomic particles in the two isotopes of bromine, 79Br and 81Br (table shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: 79Br: 35 protons, 44 neutrons, 35 electrons; 81Br: 35 protons, 46 neutrons, 35 electrons (for neutral atoms)
steps: Bromine has atomic number 35, so 35 protons in each isotope.
Neutrons = mass number - 35: 79 - 35 = 44 and 81 - 35 = 46.
Neutral atoms have 35 electrons.

questions.topic: Dot And Cross Diagram Of Br2
questions.question: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram to show the bonding in a molecule of bromine, Br2, showing only outer electrons.
questions.answer: Two Br atoms sharing one pair of electrons in a single covalent bond, each Br with three lone pairs (7 outer electrons each, 8 around each atom).
steps: Each Br has 7 outer electrons and needs 1 more to complete an octet.
The two Br atoms share one pair of electrons, forming one single covalent bond.
Each Br keeps three lone pairs, giving 8 electrons around each atom.

questions.topic: Formation Of Molecular Ion In Mass Spectrometer
questions.question: Describe the formation of the molecular ion of bromine in the mass spectrometer, including an equation (state symbols not required).
questions.answer: Gaseous Br2 molecules are bombarded with high-energy electrons, which knock one electron off each molecule to form the molecular ion: Br2 + e- -> Br2+ + 2e-.
steps: Bromine is vaporised and enters the ionisation chamber as gas-phase molecules.
High-energy electrons collide with Br2 molecules and remove one electron.
Equation: Br2 + e- -> Br2+ + 2e-, giving the molecular ion Br2+.

questions.topic: Mass Spectrum Peaks Of Bromine Molecular Ions
questions.question: On the mass spectrum grid, draw the peaks for the bromine molecular ions, showing relative peak heights. The bromine isotopes in this sample have the same relative abundance. (The grid is shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: Three peaks at m/z 158 (79Br2+), 160 (79Br81Br+) and 162 (81Br2+), with relative heights 1 : 2 : 1.
steps: Molecular ions are 79Br79Br+ (158), 79Br81Br+ (160) and 81Br81Br+ (162) with charge 1+.
With equal abundances of the isotopes, the 79Br81Br ion is formed in two ways (from 79 and 81 in either order).
So the relative heights are 1 : 2 : 1 at 158, 160 and 162.

questions.topic: Relative Molecular Mass Of Bromine Sample
questions.question: Calculate the relative molecular mass of a different bromine sample, given the percentage abundances of its isotopes (the abundance data are shown in the figure below), to two decimal places.
steps: A Br2 molecule contains two atoms, so the relative molecular mass = 2 x 79.8724 = 159.7448.
To two decimal places the relative molecular mass is 159.74.

questions.question: A stream of liquid from a burette is deflected by a charged rod. Which substance, in its liquid state, will be deflected the most? A C5H12; B CCl4; C BCl3; D CH2Cl2.
questions.answer: D (CH2Cl2)
steps: Only polar liquids are deflected by a charged rod.
C5H12, CCl4 and BCl3 are non-polar, so they are not deflected.
CH2Cl2 is a polar molecule, with two polar C-Cl bonds and two C-H bonds that do not cancel, so it is deflected the most.

questions.question: Which diagram best represents the electron density map of sodium chloride? (The diagram options are shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: A: two separate sets of contours with no shared contour, the Cl- cloud larger than the Na+ cloud
steps: Sodium chloride is ionic: the electron density is centred on the Na+ and Cl- ions with almost no density between them, so the contour lines around the two ions do not join.
Cl- is larger than Na+, so its contours should cover a bigger area; this is shown in A.
B has two equal ions, and C and D show electrons shared between the nuclei, which is covalent.

questions.question: Which molecule is polar? A CO2; B SF6; C SO2; D SiCl4.
questions.answer: C (SO2)
steps: CO2 is linear and symmetrical, so it is non-polar.
SF6 (octahedral) and SiCl4 (tetrahedral) are symmetrical, so their bond dipoles cancel.
SO2 is bent (V-shaped) and asymmetric, so it is polar.

questions.question: Which molecule is polar? A 1,1-dibromopropane; B E-1,2-dibromoethene; C hexafluoroethane; D tetrachloromethane.
questions.answer: A (1,1-dibromopropane)
steps: 1,1-dibromopropane has two Br on the same carbon, so the C-Br dipoles do not cancel.
E-1,2-dibromoethene (trans) and hexafluoroethane have symmetrical arrangements with dipoles cancelling.
Tetrachloromethane is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so it is non-polar.

questions.question: Which property shows a general decrease across the Periodic Table from sodium to chlorine? A atomic radius; B electronegativity; C first ionisation energy; D melting temperature.
questions.answer: A (atomic radius)
steps: Across Period 3, nuclear charge increases with electrons in the same shell.
This pulls the electrons closer, so atomic radius decreases.
Electronegativity and first ionisation energy increase across the period, and melting temperature peaks at Si.

questions.question: Which is a use of graphene based on its electrical properties? A drill tips; B pencils; C touch screens; D body armour.
questions.answer: C (touch screens)
steps: Graphene has delocalised electrons that move freely along its layers.
This makes it a good electrical conductor, suitable for touch screens.
Drill tips, pencils and body armour depend on hardness, softness or strength.

questions.question: What types of bonding are present in the compound ammonium chloride, NH4Cl? (The options are shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: Ionic bonding between NH4+ and Cl-, plus covalent and dative covalent bonds within the NH4+ ion.
steps: NH4Cl is made of NH4+ and Cl- ions, so the bonding between them is ionic.
Within NH4+ there are three covalent N-H bonds and one dative covalent N-H bond.
So ionic, covalent and dative covalent bonding are all present.

questions.question: Water reacts with H+ ions to form H3O+ ions. Identify the bonding within the H3O+ ion. A covalent only; B covalent and dative covalent only; C covalent, dative covalent and ionic; D ionic only.
questions.answer: B (covalent and dative covalent bonding only)
steps: In H3O+, three O-H bonds are normal covalent bonds.
The fourth O-H bond forms when O donates a lone pair to H+, a dative covalent bond.
No ionic bonding occurs within the ion itself.

questions.topic: Polarity Of C-Cl Bond And CCl4
questions.question: Which describes the polarity of the C-Cl bond and the polarity of the CCl4 molecule? (The options are shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: The C-Cl bond is polar, but the tetrahedral CCl4 molecule is non-polar because the bond dipoles cancel.
steps: Cl is more electronegative than C, so each C-Cl bond is polar.
CCl4 is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so the four dipoles cancel.
So the molecule is non-polar overall.

questions.topic: Ionic Equation For Barium Carbonate Reaction
questions.question: Write the ionic equation for BaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> BaCl2(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l). State symbols are not required.
questions.answer: BaCO3 + 2H+ -> Ba2+ + CO2 + H2O
steps: Remove spectator ions (Cl-), which appear unchanged on both sides.
Keep the species that react: BaCO3, H+ (from HCl), and the products Ba2+, CO2 and H2O.
Check: charge is 2+ on both sides; atoms balance.

questions.topic: Atom Economy Of Barium Chloride Preparation
questions.question: Calculate the atom economy by mass for the preparation of barium chloride from BaCO3 + 2HCl. Ar: H 1.0, C 12.0, O 16.0, Cl 35.5, Ba 137.3.
steps: Mr(BaCl2) = 137.3 + 71.0 = 208.3 (desired product).

questions.question: Barium chloride melts at 962 C and caesium chloride at 646 C. Explain, by considering the ions involved, the difference in melting temperatures of these Period 6 chlorides.
questions.answer: Ba2+ has a 2+ charge and is smaller than Cs+, so BaCl2 has stronger electrostatic attraction between its ions (higher lattice energy); CsCl has 1+ ions with weaker attraction, so it melts at a lower temperature.
steps: Melting temperature of an ionic compound depends on the strength of the electrostatic attraction in the lattice.
Ba2+ has a 2+ charge, so it attracts Cl- more strongly than the 1+ Cs+ does.
Ba2+ is also smaller than Cs+, which gives a higher charge density and stronger attraction.
Stronger lattice attraction means more energy to break it, so BaCl2 melts at the higher temperature.

questions.topic: Covalent Versus Ionic Character Of Chlorides
questions.question: Explain the difference in bonding between barium chloride and beryllium chloride, using the electronegativity values shown. (The electronegativity values are shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: BaCl2 is ionic (electronegativity difference 2.1), whereas BeCl2 has a smaller difference (1.5) and so has polar covalent character
steps: Ba-Cl: 3.0 - 0.9 = 2.1, a large difference, so the Cl atom takes the electrons from Ba almost completely, giving Ba2+ and Cl- ions: ionic bonding.
Be-Cl: 3.0 - 1.5 = 1.5, a smaller difference, so the electrons are shared unevenly, giving a polar covalent bond.
Be2+ is small with a high charge density, so it polarises the Cl- ion, which increases the covalent character of BeCl2.

questions.question: A solution of 7.98 g of a Group 1 sulfate M2SO4 reacts with excess BaCl2, giving 10.72 g of BaSO4. Identify the Group 1 element. Ar: Ba 137.3, S 32.1, O 16.0.
questions.answer: Potassium (K), since M2SO4 is K2SO4
steps: Moles BaSO4 = 10.72 / 233.4 = 0.0459 mol, which equals moles of M2SO4 (1 : 1).
M = 39.1, which is potassium (K2SO4).

questions.question: Complete the dot-and-cross diagram by adding all the electrons in the outer shells of the five carbon atoms in a diamond tetrahedral unit (the diagram is shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: The central C shares one electron pair with each of four outer C atoms; each outer C has 4 outer electrons, one shared with the central C and three shared with other C atoms, giving 8 electrons around every C.
steps: Each C has 4 outer electrons and forms 4 covalent bonds.
The central carbon forms one shared pair with each of the four surrounding carbons.
Each surrounding carbon also forms bonds to the rest of the lattice, so each C has 4 shared pairs (8 electrons in its outer shell).

questions.question: Draw a labelled 3D structure of graphite, showing two layers of at least 13 carbon atoms each and the forces between the layers. (The drawing is not included in the extracted text; describe the structure.)
questions.answer: Two layers of hexagonal rings of sp2 carbon atoms, each C bonded covalently to three neighbours within a layer; the layers are held together by weak van der Waals (London) forces, with delocalised electrons within each layer.
steps: Each carbon forms three covalent bonds in a flat hexagonal layer.
The fourth electron on each C is delocalised over the layer.
Layers are held apart by weak London (van der Waals) forces, which are labelled between the layers.

questions.question: Suggest why diamond has a greater density than graphite.
questions.answer: Diamond has a rigid, three-dimensional tetrahedral lattice with atoms packed more closely, whereas graphite has flat layers with large gaps between them held by weak forces.
steps: Diamond's atoms are arranged in a 3D tetrahedral network, packing tightly.
Graphite's layers are far apart because only weak London forces hold them together.
The more closely packed diamond has a greater mass per unit volume, so it is denser.

questions.topic: Deflection Of Polar And Non-Polar Liquids
questions.question: To compare polar and non-polar liquids, a stream of liquid from a burette and a positively charged plastic rod can be used. Which row of the table shows the correct direction of deflection? (The table is shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: C: polar liquids are deflected towards the rod, non-polar liquids show no deflection
steps: Polar molecules have a permanent dipole, and the molecules turn so that their delta-negative end faces the positively charged rod, which gives a net attraction and a deflection towards the rod.
Non-polar molecules have no permanent dipole, so the stream is not deflected.

questions.question: Which of these molecules are polar? I hydrogen chloride, HCl(g); II beryllium chloride, BeCl2(g); III boron trichloride, BCl3(g). A I only; B II and III; C I and III; D I, II and III.
questions.answer: A (I only)
steps: HCl is a diatomic molecule with a polar bond, so it is polar.
BeCl2 is linear and symmetrical, so its bond dipoles cancel and it is non-polar.
BCl3 is trigonal planar and symmetrical, so it is non-polar.

questions.topic: Trend In First Ionisation Energy Period 2
questions.question: Explain the general trend in first ionisation energies for the Period 2 elements.
questions.answer: First ionisation energy generally increases across Period 2 because nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same, so the outer electrons are held more strongly.
steps: Across Period 2, protons are added to the same shell.
Shielding stays about the same because electrons are added to the same shell.
Greater nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove one.

questions.question: Explain which one of the elements from lithium to nitrogen deviates from the general trend in first ionisation energy, and why.
questions.answer: Boron deviates: its first ionisation energy is lower than beryllium's, because its outer electron is in a higher-energy, more shielded 2p subshell rather than a 2s subshell.
steps: Be has outer electrons as a pair in 2s; B's outer electron is in 2p.
The 2p subshell is higher in energy than 2s and is more shielded by the 2s electrons.
So less energy is needed to remove the 2p electron of B, and its IE is lower than Be's.

questions.question: Identify the Period 3 element that has the successive ionisation energies shown (data shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: Sulfur
steps: The values rise gradually for the first six ionisations and then jump sharply from 8496 (6th) to 27 107 (7th), so there are 6 electrons in the outer shell.
An element in Period 3 with 6 outer electrons is in Group 6: sulfur (first ionisation energy about 1000 kJ mol^-1).

questions.topic: Melting Temperatures Of Period 2 Elements Diagram
questions.question: Complete the diagram by putting crosses to show the approximate melting temperatures of boron and nitrogen in the Period 2 melting temperature chart (the chart is shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: Boron: cross at about 2350 K (above Be, below C); nitrogen: cross very low, about 60 K (near the x-axis)
steps: Boron has a giant covalent structure with strong covalent bonds, so it has a very high melting temperature of about 2350 K, between that of Be (about 1550 K) and C (about 3900 K).
Nitrogen is N2, a simple molecular substance with only weak London forces between molecules, so its melting temperature is very low, about 63 K, so the cross is placed close to the zero line.

questions.question: Explain why the melting temperature of carbon is high, with reference to its structure and bonding.
questions.answer: Carbon (diamond or graphite) is a giant covalent structure in which every atom is joined to others by strong covalent bonds, so a very large amount of energy is needed to break the lattice.
steps: Carbon atoms form a giant covalent lattice with many strong C-C covalent bonds.
Melting requires breaking covalent bonds throughout the whole structure, not just weak forces between molecules.
This requires a very large amount of energy, so carbon has a very high melting temperature.

questions.question: Which statement is not correct for these Period 3 elements? A atoms of Cl(g) have the highest first ionisation energy; B ions of Cl-(g) and S2-(g) have the same ionic radius; C atoms of Na(g) have the largest atomic radius; D atoms of P(g) have the most unpaired electrons.
questions.answer: B (Cl- and S2- do not have the same ionic radius)
steps: A is correct: Cl has the highest first IE of Na to Cl (Ar is excluded).
B is incorrect: Cl- and S2- are both 18-electron ions, but S2- has fewer protons (16 vs 17), so it is larger.
C is correct: Na has the largest atomic radius in Period 3, and D is correct: P (3p3) has three unpaired electrons, the most in Period 3.

questions.question: The melting temperatures of Al, Si, P and S are shown in a table (shown in the figure below). Which element has the strongest intermolecular forces? A Al; B Si; C P; D S.
questions.answer: D: S
steps: Al and Si are not molecular: Al is a giant metallic lattice and Si is giant covalent, so they have no intermolecular forces.
Only P (P4) and S (S8) of the options are molecular, and S has the higher melting temperature (392 K compared with 317 K).
S8 molecules have more electrons than P4, so the London forces between them are stronger.
